1. Executive summary

Ledgerly is a concept mobile bank with an AI co-pilot built in. It reads a user’s spending, explains patterns in plain English, forecasts the month ahead and suggests small, safe money moves. The defining design decision is human-in-the-loop control: the AI can read and recommend, but every movement of money needs an explicit tap from the user.

Version 2 expands the product from five concept screens into a complete 11-screen flow — welcome, log in, create account, two-factor verification, password reset, home, insights, AI assistant, goals, settings and log-out confirmation — and puts the whole app through a measured WCAG 2.2 accessibility audit.

Headline result

Across eight design reviews, 13 colour-contrast failures were found and fixed. Every text style, input border and icon in the final design now meets WCAG 2.2 AA, with text contrast between 4.55:1 and 16:1.



2. My goal

I set out to answer one design question: can an AI banking assistant feel genuinely helpful while staying transparent, trustworthy and accessible to everyone? My personal goals for the project were to:

  • Solve a real problem: design for people who already use AI for money questions but cannot trust generic chatbots with their real finances.

  • Design AI responsibly: make every AI suggestion explainable and require user approval before money moves.

  • Build a complete product: go beyond hero screens to design onboarding, security, settings and edge flows.

  • Meet accessibility standards: reach WCAG 2.2 AA so the app works for users with low vision and colour-vision deficiency.

  • Show professional practice: document requirements, user stories and acceptance criteria the way a product team would.


3. The problem

3.1 Context: people already ask AI about money

Consumers have moved faster than banks. Lloyds Banking Group’s 2025 Consumer Digital Index found that 56% of UK adults — about 28.8 million people — have used AI tools for guidance on budgeting, savings, pensions or investments, and almost one in three use AI weekly to manage money. The same research links this to the UK advice gap: a full review with a traditional financial adviser costs around £1,000.

3.2 Problem statement

The core tension

People want AI help with everyday money decisions and are already using general-purpose chatbots to get it. Those tools cannot see their real accounts, carry no accountability, and around half of users doubt the answers. Banks — the source people trust most — mostly offer static charts that describe the past instead of helping plan the future. And many finance apps still fall short on accessibility, excluding users with low vision.



3.3 How might we…

  • How might we give people AI money guidance grounded in their real transactions, inside an institution they already trust?

  • How might we make AI suggestions feel helpful rather than pushy, and transparent rather than magical?

  • How might we let AI act on a user’s behalf without taking away control?

  • How might we make all of this readable and usable for people with low vision or colour-vision deficiency?

5.1 What I am trying to portray

  • Calm confidence: warm paper backgrounds, ink-black text and one deep teal accent signal a stable, trustworthy bank.

7. Screen-by-screen walkthrough

01 — Welcome

Purpose: State the promise and get users started in one tap.

  • Hero: stacked Ledgerly cards (•••• 4652, Lando Piastry) and a floating AI chip: "£86 spare this month. Move it to your Japan fund?"

  • Copy: "Banking that plans ahead." with a promise that the AI acts only with the user’s say-so.

  • Actions: "Open an account" (primary) and "I already have an account" (secondary).

Design rationale: Showing a real AI suggestion before sign-up demonstrates value instantly, and the trust promise appears in the first sentence.

02–05 — Authentication

Purpose: Secure, low-friction access that follows banking norms.

  • Log in: email and password with show/hide, a "Forgotten password" link and "New to Ledgerly? Create account".

  • Create account: username, date of birth (required for identity checks), email, password with a visible hint.

  • Verification: "Enter the 6-digit code we sent to •••• 4821", six code boxes, "Resend code (0:30)" and "Back to log in".

  • Reset password: email with inline "Send code", code entry, new and confirm password, so a reset always proves identity first.

Design rationale: White inputs with a 3.5:1 border, required-field markers and left-aligned labels make forms easy to scan and accessible.

06 — Home

Purpose: Answer "how am I doing?" in seconds and surface one useful AI action.

  • Balance card: total £4,218.60, "+£312 vs August", Current and Savings tiles.

  • Quick actions: Send, Request, Top up, Split.

  • AI suggestion: "Your groceries are £86 under budget with 9 days left. Move it to Japan trip?" with "Move £86" and "Not now".

  • Recent activity: Tesco Express −£14.35, Transport for London −£8.10.

Design rationale: One AI card at a time avoids nagging; the reason sits inside the sentence so the suggestion is explainable at a glance.

07 — Insights

Purpose: Turn spending data into understanding.

  • Summary: £1,146.20 spent, "£84 under budget", weekly chart with Saturday highlighted.

  • AI card: "Why Saturdays spike" explains late-night takeaway spending and links to Ledger AI.

  • Budgets: four categories; Dining out is flagged with the word "OVER" as well as colour.

Design rationale: Most apps stop at the chart; Ledgerly adds the "why" and a next step.

08 — Ledger AI

Purpose: Answer natural-language money questions with real data.

  • Question: "Can I afford a £600 flight to Tokyo in November?"

  • Answer: a conditional yes, plus a projected balance of £1,120 broken into Salary, Bills & rent and the flight.

  • Actions & safety: one-tap chips (dining cap, flight pot, price alerts) and "Ledger AI can make mistakes. Not regulated financial advice."

Design rationale: Showing the maths and an honest disclaimer directly addresses the 49% of users who doubt AI accuracy.

09 — Goals

Purpose: Track savings and control automation.

  • Featured goal: Japan trip £1,240 of £2,000 (62%) and "On track for 14 March at £95 a week".

  • Other goals: Emergency fund £900 of £3,000; New laptop £380 of £1,200.

  • Automations: Round-ups and Smart save (AI) toggles; "You approve every move."

Design rationale: The approval promise is repeated exactly where the user gives the AI more power.

10–11 — Settings and log out

Purpose: Give users control over their account, data and AI.

  • Settings: Personal details, Linked accounts, AI & privacy controls, Cards & limits, Security & login, Notifications, Help & support, About Ledgerly, and a red Log out.

  • Log-out modal: "Log out of Ledgerly?" with an outlined "Cancel" and a red filled "Log out" over a blurred background.

Design rationale: Destructive actions are visually distinct and always confirmed, preventing accidental log-outs.

8. User stories and acceptance criteria

Written in the standard "As a… I want… so that…" format, with acceptance criteria in Given / When / Then form so they can be tested.

ID

User story

Acceptance criteria

US-01

As a new user, I want to open an account quickly so that I can start banking without visiting a branch.

Given I am on Welcome, when I tap "Open an account" and complete username, date of birth, email and password, then I am sent to Verification. Required fields show an error message if left empty.

US-02

As a returning user, I want to log in securely so that my money is protected.

Given valid credentials, when I tap "Log in", then I am asked for a 6-digit code. Given a correct code, when I tap "Confirm", then Home loads within 2 seconds.

US-03

As a user who forgot my password, I want to reset it safely so that I can regain access.

Given I enter my email and tap "Send code", then a code is emailed. I can only set a new password after entering a valid code. "Resend code" becomes available after 30 seconds.

US-04

As a saver, I want the app to spot spare money so that I can reach my goals faster.

Given I am under budget in a category, when I open Home, then one AI suggestion shows the amount and reason. Tapping "Move £86" asks me to confirm; "Not now" dismisses it.

US-05

As a user, I want to understand why my spending changed so that I can change my habits.

Given spending is higher on a day, when I open Insights, then that day is highlighted and an AI card explains the cause in plain English. Over-budget categories show the word "OVER".

US-06

As a user, I want to ask whether I can afford something so that I make confident decisions.

Given I type a question in Ledger AI, then the answer shows a projected balance and its breakdown. A "Show my assumptions" link is always present, and so is the disclaimer.

US-07

As a user, I want to control automations so that nothing happens without my consent.

Given I am on Goals, when I tap a toggle, then its state changes and is announced to screen readers. No AI money movement happens without my approval.

US-08

As a user, I want to log out safely so that nobody else can access my account.

Given I tap "Log out" in Settings, then a confirmation modal appears. "Cancel" returns me to Settings; "Log out" ends my session and returns me to Welcome.

US-09

As a user with low vision, I want all text to be readable so that I can use the app independently.

Given any screen, then all text meets 4.5:1 contrast and all input borders and icons meet 3:1 (WCAG 2.2 AA).

11. Technical architecture

The architecture separates reading from acting. The AI service can read transactions and propose actions, but proposals pass through a guardrails layer and an approval queue; only the user’s confirmation releases a request to the core banking ledger.

Figure 4 — Proposed system architecture

Layer

Proposed technology

Mobile app

React Native with TypeScript; Figma colour tokens map to a shared theme file

API & auth

API gateway with OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect, one-time codes and biometric login

Data

Core banking ledger plus Open Banking account-information access

AI service

Large language model with retrieval over categorised transactions, plus a deterministic forecasting engine for numbers

Guardrails

PII redaction, policy checks, no write action without approval

Observability

Audit log of every AI suggestion and user decision

Table 9 — Proposed stack

Why numbers come from a forecasting engine: language models can make arithmetic errors, so balances like "£1,120 on 30 Nov" are calculated deterministically and the model only explains them.

13.2 Colour theory

  • Psychology of teal: blue-green blends the trust and stability associated with blue with the growth and prosperity associated with green — ideal for money. It also differentiates Ledgerly from the coral, pink and bright blue common among UK challenger banks.

  • Complementary contrast: warm amber sits opposite teal on the colour wheel, so AI moments stand out instantly without clashing.

  • 60-30-10 rule: roughly 60% warm neutrals (paper and white), 30% ink for text and dark cards, and 10% teal and amber accents, keeping the interface calm with clear focal points.

  • Warm neutrals: paper and ink instead of pure white and black reduce glare and create an editorial, considered feel.

  • Semantic colour: red is reserved for destructive actions, amber for AI and warnings, teal for primary actions and positive progress.

13.3 How I applied colour theory

Principle

Where it appears in Ledgerly

One accent, used sparingly

Teal marks only the primary button, active tab, progress and featured goal — so the eye always knows what to do next

A colour that means "AI"

Amber appears only on AI labels, the AI chip, the "Why Saturdays spike" icon and the Smart save tag

Light vs dark surfaces

Dark ink cards carry high-emphasis content (balance, AI insight, settings); separate secondary greys were defined for light (#5F636A) and dark (#A4A9B1) surfaces after the audit showed one grey could not pass on both

Destructive red

Log out uses #EB5757 on dark and a #B42318 filled button in the modal, distinct from every other link

Never colour alone

Over-budget shows the word "OVER"; income uses "+"; toggles change knob position; AI items carry a text label

Table 13 — Colour theory in practice

13.4 Typography, icons and components

  • Typography: a clean sans-serif for headings, balances and body text keeps figures crisp and legible; the Fraunces serif is reserved for the Ledgerly wordmark to give the brand an editorial signature. Scale: 28–44 px titles and balances, 16–18 px section headings, 13–16 px body, 12 px captions.

  • Icons: line icons on a 24 px grid with rounded caps, matching the soft card corners; the four-point sparkle is reserved for AI.

  • Components: rounded cards (20–26 px radius), 52 px inputs and primary buttons, pill chips, and toggles with clear on/off positions.


14. WCAG 2.2 accessibility audit

Verdict: the app meets WCAG 2.2 AA for all criteria that can be verified in a visual design

Every text style on all 11 screens meets the 4.5:1 minimum, every input border and icon meets 3:1, and meaning is never conveyed by colour alone. Criteria that depend on code (screen-reader names, focus order, text resizing) are specified as developer handoff requirements below.

14.2 Before and after

Figure 5 — Every element moved from failing to passing the AA minimum

14.3 Audit journey

Figure 6 — Failures per review: progress was not linear

The count rose in Review 6 because new elements (input borders, hints, placeholders, a modal subtitle) were introduced with a light grey that had not been checked. Defining separate colour tokens for light and dark surfaces, then applying them layer by layer, brought failures to zero in Review 8.

14.4 Developer handoff for full conformance

  • Give every icon-only button an accessible name (for example "Notifications", "Show password", "Voice input", "Send").

  • Trap focus in the log-out modal, close it with Escape, and show a visible focus outline on every interactive element.

  • Support iOS Dynamic Type and Android font scaling without clipping text.

  • Let the 6-digit code accept paste and SMS autofill.

  • Show form errors as text, not only as a red border, and announce toggle state changes.


15. Visual design review

Viewed as a whole, Ledgerly has a coherent, premium and calm visual language:

  • Two moods, one system: dark onboarding screens create a focused, secure first impression; light core screens feel open and readable for daily use. Shared cards, radii and teal accents tie them together.

  • Clear hierarchy: large balances and titles, one primary teal button per area, and secondary actions in outlined or text styles.

  • Recognisable AI: the amber sparkle makes AI content identifiable at a glance on every screen.

  • Consistency: the same bottom navigation, header pattern, card style and spacing appear across all core screens.

  • Areas to refine: removing the hamburger menu (duplicated by the tab bar), back arrows on top-level tab screens, and a handful of copy details listed in Section 18.

17.2 Key lessons

  • Accessibility must be measured, not judged by eye. Several greys looked fine on screen but failed at 2–3:1. Checking ratios is the only reliable method.

  • Use colour tokens from day one. Changing colours layer by layer caused regressions; Figma variables such as text/secondary and text/secondary-on-dark would have prevented them.

  • One grey cannot serve every surface. Text that passes on cream fails on black, so light and dark surfaces need their own secondary colours.

  • Design reviews are iterative. Fixing one area can introduce issues elsewhere; re-checking the whole app each round is essential.

  • Copy and logic matter as much as visuals. Small details — a balance that does not add up, "Sign in" on a sign-up form, a password reset without verification — undermine trust in a finance product.

  • Trust is a design feature. Visual calm, consistent AI signalling, explainable answers and mandatory approval all serve the same goal.

18. Next steps

  • Run moderated usability tests with five participants and replace hypotheses with real findings.

  • Final copy polish: "Create account" on the sign-up button, Current balance £2,978.60 so the total adds up, "£42 / £50", "Ledger AI" header, and matching Settings icons.

  • Simplify navigation: remove the hamburger and back arrows on tab screens; open Settings from the profile avatar.

  • Convert colours into Figma variables and rename frames for developer handoff.

  • Design error, empty, offline and dark-mode states.


19. Overall review

Ledgerly demonstrates the full arc of a product design project: an evidence-based problem, a clear and responsible AI concept, a complete 11-screen flow, documented requirements and testable user stories, and a measured accessibility audit that took the design from 13 contrast failures to full WCAG 2.2 AA compliance.
